data.title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
data.abstract: Automated red teaming holds substantial promise for uncovering and mitigating the risks associated with the malicious use of large language models (LLMs), yet the field lacks a standardized evaluation framework to rigorously assess new methods. To address this issue, we introduce HarmBench, a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming. We identify several desirable properties previously unaccounted for in red teaming evaluations and systematically design HarmBench to meet these criteria. Using HarmBench, we conduct a large-scale comparison of 18 red teaming methods and 33 target LLMs and defenses, yielding novel insights. We also introduce a highly efficient adversarial training method that greatly enhances LLM robustness across a wide range of attacks, demonstrating how HarmBench enables codevelopment of attacks and defenses. We open source HarmBench at https://github.com/centerforaisafety/HarmBench.
data.tldr: HarmBench standardizes automated red-teaming evaluation across attack methods, target models, and defenses. Its benchmark compares 18 red-teamers and 33 target LLMs, while enabling adversarial training that improves refusal robustness across diverse attacks.
suggested_questions: How does HarmBench standardize automated red teaming evaluations?
How does HarmBench compare the 18 red teaming methods?
How does adversarial training improve robustness against HarmBench attacks?

preview.name: Red Teaming
preview.description: Red teaming is the practice of adversarially probing an AI system to discover harmful, unsafe or otherwise undesired behavior before deployment, borrowing the term from military and computer-security exercises in which a red team plays the attacker. For language models, human red teamers write prompts that try to elicit toxic content, dangerous instructions, privacy leaks, bias or policy violation
